## Predicting observations the model did not see

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/index/04-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/index.qmd; note-sha256: e76b4af25084d86f72021b24271a8f45a0ddce7a7cd47882ec73f32e6b0ec8c9; role: concept -->

Predictive evaluation must therefore specify the unit held out during fitting.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An observed-minus-fitted residual describes a response used to estimate a model. It does not tell us how the complete procedure will predict a response unavailable during fitting. In Natural Stories, unavailable can mean one response row, every response from one participant, or every position in one story. Predictive evaluation must therefore specify the unit held out during fitting.

## Defining and scoring a prediction

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/index/07-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/index.qmd; note-sha256: e76b4af25084d86f72021b24271a8f45a0ddce7a7cd47882ec73f32e6b0ec8c9; role: concept -->

The bias--variance tradeoff explains why a procedure can closely fit one training sample yet vary across samples.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Prediction targets state which responses or groups are new and which predictors remain available. Training and test data then enforce that separation, including training-only estimation of predictor transformations. A predictive loss scores each held-out prediction. The bias--variance tradeoff explains why a procedure can closely fit one training sample yet vary across samples.

[Sources]

https://github.com/languageMIT/naturalstories/tree/4700daad696e942f5aba23c957a7423d0de66612
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-020-09503-7
:::

Comparing predictive loss moves to MegaOrientation and evaluates additive and frame-specific ordinal models on verbs absent from fitting. ## Natural Stories

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets/04-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd; note-sha256: c23546d94a4f50e869c016cae9ce824d5a707bcac0eae5565a85eff03151c8e2; role: concept -->

We use the corrected Natural Stories release, introduced and validated by Futrell et al. (2021), throughout the first six pages of this unit.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We use the corrected Natural Stories release, introduced and validated by Futrell et al. (2021), throughout the first six pages of this unit. The corpus contains English stories enriched for low-frequency syntactic constructions, self-paced reading times, and aligned lexical annotations. The corrected release fixes a one-position displacement in the reading-time records. Its preprocessing excludes reader-story passes with fewer than five correct comprehension answers and reading times outside the release's 100-to-3,000-ms window.

## Three prediction targets {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets/08-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd; note-sha256: c23546d94a4f50e869c016cae9ce824d5a707bcac0eae5565a85eff03151c8e2; role: math -->

All three procedures used later fit the population regression

$$
\log RT_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1z(L_i)+\beta_2z(F_i)+\beta_3z(S_i)+\epsilon_i,
$$

where $L_i$ is word length, $F_i$ is log unigram frequency, and $S_i$ is released GPT-3 surprisal.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

All three procedures used later fit the population regression

$$

=
\beta_0+\beta_1z(L_i)+\beta_2z(F_i)+\beta_3z(S_i)+\epsilon_i,
$$

where $L_i$ is word length, $F_i$ is log unigram frequency, and $S_i$ is released GPT-3 surprisal.

## Three prediction targets

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets/11-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd; note-sha256: c23546d94a4f50e869c016cae9ce824d5a707bcac0eae5565a85eff03151c8e2; role: concept -->

A story split evaluates one omitted member of these deliberately enriched texts.

::: {.notes}

These separations ask different questions. A random row split evaluates another response from the represented collection of readers and stories. A participant split evaluates a reader absent from fitting. A story split evaluates one omitted member of these deliberately enriched texts.

Leave-one-story-out results consequently describe these ten omissions; they do not estimate performance for an unrestricted population of English texts.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The story target needs especially narrow wording. The corpus supplies 10 opportunities to inspect an omitted story, not 846,537 independent story transfers. Leave-one-story-out results consequently describe these ten omissions; they do not estimate performance for an unrestricted population of English texts.

## The prediction information set

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets/13-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd; note-sha256: c23546d94a4f50e869c016cae9ce824d5a707bcac0eae5565a85eff03151c8e2; role: concept -->

A held-out story contributes its lexical predictors but no response from any of its positions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Holding out a group does not by itself determine which information about it may be used. In these analyses, a held-out row keeps its word length, frequency, and surprisal because those predictors are available at prediction time. A held-out participant contributes no reading-time response to fitting. A held-out story contributes its lexical predictors but no response from any of its positions.

[Sources]

https://github.com/languageMIT/naturalstories/tree/4700daad696e942f5aba23c957a7423d0de66612

## The prediction information set

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets/14-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd; note-sha256: c23546d94a4f50e869c016cae9ce824d5a707bcac0eae5565a85eff03151c8e2; role: concept -->

A separately estimated test center would place the test observations in a different coordinate system.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The preprocessing rule is part of the information set. Each predictor mean and standard deviation is estimated from training rows and then applied to test rows. A full-data center would let held-out predictor values affect the training representation. A separately estimated test center would place the test observations in a different coordinate system.

## Theory determines what should be held out

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets/15-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd; note-sha256: c23546d94a4f50e869c016cae9ce824d5a707bcac0eae5565a85eff03151c8e2; role: concept -->

A claim about connected text requires story folds and enough story-level replication to support it.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The most demanding split is not automatically the right one. A reading model used for an already represented reader may reasonably target another response row. A claim about transfer across readers requires participant folds. A claim about connected text requires story folds and enough story-level replication to support it.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
https://github.com/languageMIT/naturalstories/tree/4700daad696e942f5aba23c957a7423d0de66612

## Theory determines what should be held out

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets/16-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd; note-sha256: c23546d94a4f50e869c016cae9ce824d5a707bcac0eae5565a85eff03151c8e2; role: concept -->

Predictive evaluation establishes performance for a stated response, information set, split, and population; the mechanism requires additional evidence.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Successful prediction also does not establish a processing mechanism. Word surprisal can improve a held-out score without showing that readers internally represent the fitted language model's probabilities. Predictive evaluation establishes performance for a stated response, information set, split, and population; the mechanism requires additional evidence.

## Training and test data

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data/03-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.qmd; note-sha256: c05ae41abad7fbf34fa3ae3cbb1b194a7524071d2e7fc672e9c298a14ba9772d; role: concept -->

Training fit thus cannot by itself estimate predictive loss for a reader absent during fitting.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The residuals of a fitted regression are observed-minus-fitted discrepancies on the observations used to estimate its coefficients. A flexible model can reduce those residuals by following features of the training responses that will not recur. Training fit thus cannot by itself estimate predictive loss for a reader absent during fitting.

[Sources]

https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage
:::

## The separation rule {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data/04-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.qmd; note-sha256: c05ae41abad7fbf34fa3ae3cbb1b194a7524071d2e7fc672e9c298a14ba9772d; role: math -->

Let $D_{\mathrm{train}}$ and $D_{\mathrm{test}}$ be disjoint collections of observations. A fitted predictor is

$$
\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{train}}
=
\operatorname{Fit}(D_{\mathrm{train}}),
$$

and test loss is

$$
\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{test}}
=
\frac{1}{|D_{\mathrm{test}}|}
\sum_{i\in D_{\mathrm{test}}}
L\left(y_i,\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{train}}(x_i)\right).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $D_{\mathrm{train}}$ and $D_{\mathrm{test}}$ be disjoint collections of observations. A fitted predictor is

$$
\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{train}}
=
\operatorname{Fit}(D_{\mathrm{train}}),
$$

and test loss is

$$
\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{test}}
=
\frac{1}{|D_{\mathrm{test}}|}
\sum_{i\in D_{\mathrm{test}}}
L\left(y_i,\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{train}}(x_i)\right).
$$

[Sources]

https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage
:::

Test responses must not influence the coefficients, predictor transformations, model choice, or any other fitted quantity used to produce their predictions.

## Leakage through preprocessing

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data/10-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.qmd; note-sha256: c05ae41abad7fbf34fa3ae3cbb1b194a7524071d2e7fc672e9c298a14ba9772d; role: concept -->

Directly fitting on a test response is one case, but preprocessing can leak more quietly.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

**Data leakage** occurs when information from the test set influences a fitted decision that should have been made without it. Directly fitting on a test response is one case, but preprocessing can leak more quietly.

[Sources]

https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage
:::

## Leakage through preprocessing

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data/11-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.qmd; note-sha256: c05ae41abad7fbf34fa3ae3cbb1b194a7524071d2e7fc672e9c298a14ba9772d; role: concept -->

- Averaging reading times over readers before holding readers out carries their responses into the target.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

- Centering a predictor using the complete dataset lets held-out predictor values affect the training representation. - Imputing a missing test response from a full-data mean uses held-out responses. - Selecting predictors by their full-data response correlation consults the test set. - Choosing a model because it has the best test score turns the test data into selection data. - Averaging reading times over readers before holding readers out carries their responses into the target.

[Sources]

https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage
:::

$$
z_i=\frac{x_i-\overline{x}_{\mathrm{train}}}{s_{\mathrm{train}}}
$$

for both training and test observations.

::: {.notes}

## One split and repeated decisions

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data/14-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.qmd; note-sha256: c05ae41abad7fbf34fa3ae3cbb1b194a7524071d2e7fc672e9c298a14ba9772d; role: concept -->

Cross-validation rotates the test role so that every observation receives a held-out prediction.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A single split combines model performance with the composition of one test set. Increasing the test fraction provides more evaluation responses but fewer fitting responses; decreasing it has the opposite effect. Cross-validation rotates the test role so that every observation receives a held-out prediction.

[Sources]

https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage
:::

A three-way split or nested cross-validation keeps final test responses outside both coefficient fitting and model selection.

::: {.notes}

The test set is also not a renewable source of decisions. If several specifications are compared on these responses and the best is selected, its reported score is optimistic. ## Predictive loss

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss/02-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: c07bdedc720ada5bbc8decae0504079cae4c0ccc23e483cb9b05aefef8a6afac; role: concept -->

These choices determine which misses receive the most weight and which empirical units receive equal influence.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The training-and-test page produced predictions for readers absent during fitting. An evaluation still needs a loss function and an averaging unit. These choices determine which misses receive the most weight and which empirical units receive equal influence.

[Sources]

https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html
:::

## Predictive loss

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss/03-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: c07bdedc720ada5bbc8decae0504079cae4c0ccc23e483cb9b05aefef8a6afac; role: concept -->

A held-out mean loss estimates that expectation for the split and averaging unit stated by the analysis.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **loss function** $L(y,\widehat y)$ assigns a nonnegative cost to predicting $\widehat y$ when the observed response is $y$. The **predictive risk** is expected loss on new responses from the population under study. A held-out mean loss estimates that expectation for the split and averaging unit stated by the analysis.

[Sources]

https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html
:::

## Squared and absolute loss {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss/04-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: c07bdedc720ada5bbc8decae0504079cae4c0ccc23e483cb9b05aefef8a6afac; role: math -->

The **squared-error loss** is

$$
L_{\mathrm{SE}}(y,\widehat y)=(y-\widehat y)^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **squared-error loss** is

$$
L_{\mathrm{SE}}(y,\widehat y)=(y-\widehat y)^2.
$$

[Sources]

https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html
:::

## Squared and absolute loss {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss/05-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: c07bdedc720ada5bbc8decae0504079cae4c0ccc23e483cb9b05aefef8a6afac; role: math -->

Over $N$ held-out predictions, mean squared error and root mean squared error are

$$
\operatorname{MSE}
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2,
\qquad
\operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{\operatorname{MSE}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Over $N$ held-out predictions, mean squared error and root mean squared error are

$$
\operatorname{MSE}
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2,
\qquad
\operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{\operatorname{MSE}}.
$$

[Sources]

https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html

## Squared and absolute loss

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss/06-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: c07bdedc720ada5bbc8decae0504079cae4c0ccc23e483cb9b05aefef8a6afac; role: concept -->

The conditional mean is the optimal point prediction under squared loss.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Squaring gives large errors disproportionate influence. Taking the root returns the score to the response scale. For Natural Stories, that scale is log reading time, not milliseconds. The conditional mean is the optimal point prediction under squared loss.

[Sources]

https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html

## Squared and absolute loss {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss/07-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: c07bdedc720ada5bbc8decae0504079cae4c0ccc23e483cb9b05aefef8a6afac; role: math -->

The **absolute-error loss** is

$$
L_{\mathrm{AE}}(y,\widehat y)=|y-\widehat y|,
$$

with held-out average

$$
\operatorname{MAE}
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N|y_i-\widehat y_i|.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **absolute-error loss** is

$$
L_{\mathrm{AE}}(y,\widehat y)=|y-\widehat y|,
$$

with held-out average

$$
\operatorname{MAE}
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N|y_i-\widehat y_i|.
$$

[Sources]

https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html
:::

Reporting RMSE and MAE can expose sensitivity to large errors, but the analysis should still designate a primary loss before comparing models.

::: {.notes}

Absolute loss grows linearly, and the conditional median is its optimal point prediction. Reporting RMSE and MAE can expose sensitivity to large errors, but the analysis should still designate a primary loss before comparing models.

## Loss is not explanatory adequacy

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss/13-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: c07bdedc720ada5bbc8decae0504079cae4c0ccc23e483cb9b05aefef8a6afac; role: concept -->

Prediction evaluates a specified mapping from available information to responses under a stated separation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Lower predictive loss does not show that a predictor is causal or that a reader internally computes the fitted predictor. In this regression, lower loss from GPT-3 surprisal would not isolate lexical expectation from correlated properties of words and contexts. Prediction evaluates a specified mapping from available information to responses under a stated separation.

[Sources]

https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html
:::

## Loss is not explanatory adequacy

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss/14-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: c07bdedc720ada5bbc8decae0504079cae4c0ccc23e483cb9b05aefef8a6afac; role: concept -->

Predictive loss thus addresses an additional question rather than replacing parameter interpretation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Conversely, a theoretically meaningful coefficient can contribute little to held-out prediction. A small, stable association may be estimable while accounting for little response variation. Predictive loss thus addresses an additional question rather than replacing parameter interpretation.

[Sources]

https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html
:::

## Prediction bias and prediction variance

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/03-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: concept -->

The **bias-variance decomposition** separates these two failure modes.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A linear reading-time model may miss curvature in the association among length, frequency, surprisal, and mean response. A more flexible model may instead follow sample-specific variation. The **bias-variance decomposition** separates these two failure modes.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Beginning with repeated training samples {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/04-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: math -->

At a fixed predictor vector $x$, let the response be generated by

$$
Y=f(x)+\varepsilon,
$$

where $f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ and

$$
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=\sigma^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

At a fixed predictor vector $x$, let the response be generated by

$$
Y=f(x)+\varepsilon,
$$

where $f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ and

$$
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=\sigma^2.
$$

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Beginning with repeated training samples

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/05-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: concept -->

It does not describe variation among observed responses with the same predictors.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Repeatedly drawing a comparable training sample and applying the same complete fitting procedure produces a different $\widehat f(x)$ on each repetition. Prediction variance describes variation among those learned predictions. It does not describe variation among observed responses with the same predictors.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Beginning with repeated training samples {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/06-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: math -->

The bias and prediction variance are

$$
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f(x))
=
\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]-f(x)
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat f(x)]
=
\mathbb{E}\left[
  \left(\widehat f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]\right)^2
\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The bias and prediction variance are

$$
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f(x))
=
\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]-f(x)
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat f(x)]
=
\mathbb{E}\left[
  \left(\widehat f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]\right)^2
\right].
$$

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Deriving the decomposition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/07-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: math -->

We want expected squared error for a new response at the fixed predictor vector:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\widehat f(x))^2\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We want expected squared error for a new response at the fixed predictor vector:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\widehat f(x))^2\right].
$$

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Deriving the decomposition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/08-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: math -->

Add and subtract both $f(x)$ and $\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]$:

$$
Y-\widehat f(x)
=
\underbrace{Y-f(x)}_{\text{response noise}}
+
\underbrace{f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]}_{\text{negative bias}}
+
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]-\widehat f(x)}_{\text{training-sample variation}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Add and subtract both $f(x)$ and $\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]$:

$$
Y-\widehat f(x)
=
\underbrace{Y-f(x)}_{\text{response noise}}
+
\underbrace{f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]}_{\text{negative bias}}
+
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]-\widehat f(x)}_{\text{training-sample variation}}.
$$

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Deriving the decomposition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/09-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: math -->

After squaring, the expected cross-products are zero because the response noise has mean zero and the fitted predictions are centered around their own expectation. Thus,

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\widehat f(x))^2\right]
=
\sigma^2
+
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f(x))^2
+
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat f(x)].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

After squaring, the expected cross-products are zero because the response noise has mean zero and the fitted predictions are centered around their own expectation. Thus,

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\widehat f(x))^2\right]
=
\sigma^2
+
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f(x))^2
+
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat f(x)].
$$

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Deriving the decomposition

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/10-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: concept -->

The other two terms depend on the complete learning procedure.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The first term is **irreducible error** under the declared data-generating process. The other two terms depend on the complete learning procedure.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## An empirically calibrated Natural Stories simulation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/11-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: concept -->

Each repetition samples actual positions with replacement and adds a residual resampled from that empirical fit.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

True bias is not identified from one observed corpus. We thus use the only simulation in this module and label its assumptions. the calculation loads the Natural Stories data, averages responses and predictors to observed story positions, fits a cubic reference surface, and declares that fitted surface to be the simulation truth. Each repetition samples actual positions with replacement and adds a residual resampled from that empirical fit.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## What the simulation establishes

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/16-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: concept -->

The cubic reference surface is assumed true for the exercise; another calibrated truth could change the comparison.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This calibration demonstrates the decomposition using observed predictor values, response scale, and residuals. It does not estimate the unknown Natural Stories data-generating process. The cubic reference surface is assumed true for the exercise; another calibrated truth could change the comparison.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## What the simulation establishes

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff/17-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd; note-sha256: be5427f80a0718be5dfeab17101c7fdd248a811ce5b3f9652926c7b40afa4932; role: concept -->

Held-out loss can evaluate their combined consequence, but it cannot identify separate bias and variance terms without an assumption about $f(x)$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The example also shows why coefficient count is not a definition of prediction variance. Regularization, sample size, preprocessing, and the predictor distribution all affect how much a procedure changes across training samples. Held-out loss can evaluate their combined consequence, but it cannot identify separate bias and variance terms without an assumption about $f(x)$.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

**$K$-fold cross-validation (CV)** reduces dependence on a single partition by rotating which fold serves as the test set.

## Cross-validation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation/03-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 5cb4a2f5e855e985fabc6f485b51c1a0ba8d0d235e36696e65f304cdf1d7ca5e; role: concept -->

This does not make its reader or story new as well; the fold construction determines which units cross the training-test boundary.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The output is one out-of-fold prediction for every observation. Each prediction comes from a fit that excluded that response. This does not make its reader or story new as well; the fold construction determines which units cross the training-test boundary.

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation/05-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 5cb4a2f5e855e985fabc6f485b51c1a0ba8d0d235e36696e65f304cdf1d7ca5e; role: concept -->

## The algorithm {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation/06-list; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 5cb4a2f5e855e985fabc6f485b51c1a0ba8d0d235e36696e65f304cdf1d7ca5e; role: list -->

Partition observation indices into disjoint folds $F_1,\ldots,F_K$. For fold $k$:

1. Fit the complete procedure to observations outside $F_k$;
2. Use that fitted procedure to predict observations in $F_k$; and
3. Store the predictions in their original rows.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Partition observation indices into disjoint folds $F_1,\ldots,F_K$. For fold $k$: fit the complete procedure to observations outside $F_k$. use that fitted procedure to predict observations in $F_k$; and store the predictions in their original rows.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

## The algorithm {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation/07-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 5cb4a2f5e855e985fabc6f485b51c1a0ba8d0d235e36696e65f304cdf1d7ca5e; role: math -->

After every fold has been processed,

$$
\widehat R_{\mathrm{CV}}
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{k=1}^K
\sum_{i\in F_k}
L\left(y_i,\widehat f_{-k}(x_i)\right),
$$

where $\widehat f_{-k}$ is fit without fold $k$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

After every fold has been processed,

$$
\widehat R_{\mathrm{CV}}
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{k=1}^K
\sum_{i\in F_k}
L\left(y_i,\widehat f_{-k}(x_i)\right),
$$

where $\widehat f_{-k}$ is fit without fold $k$.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

## Every fitted decision stays inside the loop

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation/13-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 5cb4a2f5e855e985fabc6f485b51c1a0ba8d0d235e36696e65f304cdf1d7ca5e; role: concept -->

A tuning parameter requires an inner validation loop if it adapts to responses; the outer prediction then evaluates the complete selection rule.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Cross-validation evaluates the complete procedure, not just its final coefficient formula. Centering, scaling, feature selection, imputation, and penalty tuning must be repeated using only each training portion. A tuning parameter requires an inner validation loop if it adapts to responses; the outer prediction then evaluates the complete selection rule.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

The Natural Stories code has no tuning step: its predictor set and fold seed are fixed, but its training moments and regression coefficients remain fold-specific.

## What $K$ changes

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation/15-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 5cb4a2f5e855e985fabc6f485b51c1a0ba8d0d235e36696e65f304cdf1d7ca5e; role: concept -->

Fewer folds cost less computation but fit on less of the data for each prediction.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

With larger $K$, each model uses a larger training fraction and a smaller test fold. Leave-one-out CV sets $K=N$ for row-level omission. Fewer folds cost less computation but fit on less of the data for each prediction.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

## What $K$ changes

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation/16-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 5cb4a2f5e855e985fabc6f485b51c1a0ba8d0d235e36696e65f304cdf1d7ca5e; role: concept -->

Randomly creating more row folds cannot manufacture additional story-level replication.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Fold count is a design setting, not a probability law. If the scientific target is an omitted story, the ten story identifiers naturally define ten held-out groups. Randomly creating more row folds cannot manufacture additional story-level replication.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

A test applied to fold means would treat computational partitions as if they were sampling units.

[Transcript]

The five fits reuse most of their training rows. Their losses are consequently not five independent studies. A test applied to fold means would treat computational partitions as if they were sampling units.

## Grouped cross-validation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation/02-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 0873b064c7ddaa02659701837b5e2eadcb70b453b443c0d37ed4a37e03069ef1; role: concept -->

**Grouped $K$-fold cross-validation** instead assigns every row from a group to the same fold.

::: {.notes}

The cross-validation page placed response rows into random folds. The same reader and story consequently occurred in both training and test data. **Grouped $K$-fold cross-validation** instead assigns every row from a group to the same fold.

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation/03-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 0873b064c7ddaa02659701837b5e2eadcb70b453b443c0d37ed4a37e03069ef1; role: concept -->

Holding out a story evaluates one omitted member of the ten construction-enriched texts.

::: {.notes}

The Natural Stories introduction fixed participant and story as two candidate grouping units. Holding out participants evaluates new readers of the represented stories. Holding out a story evaluates one omitted member of the ten construction-enriched texts.

## Constructing grouped folds {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation/04-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 0873b064c7ddaa02659701837b5e2eadcb70b453b443c0d37ed4a37e03069ef1; role: math -->

Let $g(i)$ be the group containing observation $i$. Grouped validation requires

$$
g(i)=g(j)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{fold}(i)=\operatorname{fold}(j).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $g(i)$ be the group containing observation $i$. Grouped validation requires

$$
g(i)=g(j)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{fold}(i)=\operatorname{fold}(j).
$$

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html#cross-validation-iterators-for-grouped-data

## Participant and story validation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation/09-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 0873b064c7ddaa02659701837b5e2eadcb70b453b443c0d37ed4a37e03069ef1; role: concept -->

Showing all story points prevents a pooled claim from concealing this heterogeneity.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Adding surprisal lowers leave-one-story-out RMSE for stories 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 and raises it for stories 2, 6, 8, 9, 10. The changes range from -0.000145 to 0.000205 log-time units. Showing all story points prevents a pooled claim from concealing this heterogeneity.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html#cross-validation-iterators-for-grouped-data
:::

## Group-weighted scores {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation/10-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 0873b064c7ddaa02659701837b5e2eadcb70b453b443c0d37ed4a37e03069ef1; role: math -->

For group $g$ with $n_g$ responses, define

$$
\overline L_g
=
\frac{1}{n_g}
\sum_{i:g(i)=g}L(y_i,\widehat y_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For group $g$ with $n_g$ responses, define

$$
\overline L_g
=
\frac{1}{n_g}
\sum_{i:g(i)=g}L(y_i,\widehat y_i).
$$

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation/11-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 0873b064c7ddaa02659701837b5e2eadcb70b453b443c0d37ed4a37e03069ef1; role: math -->

A group-weighted score is

$$
\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^G\overline L_g.
$$

## Group-weighted scores

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation/12-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 0873b064c7ddaa02659701837b5e2eadcb70b453b443c0d37ed4a37e03069ef1; role: concept -->

The latter may be useful for corpus prediction, but its uncertainty cannot treat positions from one story as independent story transfers.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Each group receives equal weight. A row-weighted score instead pools all responses before averaging. The latter may be useful for corpus prediction, but its uncertainty cannot treat positions from one story as independent story transfers.

## Group leakage and limits

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation/13-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 0873b064c7ddaa02659701837b5e2eadcb70b453b443c0d37ed4a37e03069ef1; role: concept -->

For that reason, this analysis retains participant-level response rows and fits predictor transformations inside folds.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Moving rows together does not prevent leakage from a response-derived predictor constructed before the split. A word-position mean reading time computed across all participants would contain the test participants' responses. For that reason, this analysis retains participant-level response rows and fits predictor transformations inside folds.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html#cross-validation-iterators-for-grouped-data
:::

## Group leakage and limits

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation/14-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 0873b064c7ddaa02659701837b5e2eadcb70b453b443c0d37ed4a37e03069ef1; role: concept -->

They do not license generalization to arbitrary English stories.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The participant model remains a population regression without participant or story effects. It is designed to expose the difference among targets, not to reproduce the mixed-effects validation in Futrell et al. The story results concern ten omitted enriched texts. They do not license generalization to arbitrary English stories.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html#cross-validation-iterators-for-grouped-data
:::

## MegaOrientation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/comparing-predictive-loss/04-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/comparing-predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: ce68be05102e6e996f44b908b48670e50377114a9229081029c3a74d95000f21; role: concept -->

The corrected MegaOrientation v1.1 release changes the released participant and verb inventories after items with irregular-inflection errors were rerun.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Moon and White (2020) constructed sentence pairs that force past- or future-oriented interpretations by combining matrix tense or modality with an incompatible embedded temporal adverb. Participants rated the sentences on a 1-to-7 acceptability scale. The corrected MegaOrientation v1.1 release changes the released participant and verb inventories after items with irregular-inflection errors were rerun.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/005282/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-orientation/mega-orientation-v1.1.zip
:::

## MegaOrientation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/comparing-predictive-loss/05-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/comparing-predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: ce68be05102e6e996f44b908b48670e50377114a9229081029c3a74d95000f21; role: concept -->

Thus, the target is an unseen verb within the selected multi-frame inventory, not a reproduction of the paper's latent-type comparison.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The original paper fits latent lexical, structural, and mixed models with participant-specific ordinal cutpoints. The teaching comparison is narrower. It restricts the release to verbs attested in at least two frames, fits population cumulative-logit models, and holds out every response from a verb together. Thus, the target is an unseen verb within the selected multi-frame inventory, not a reproduction of the paper's latent-type comparison.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/005282/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-orientation/mega-orientation-v1.1.zip
:::

$$

## Scope of the gain

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/comparing-predictive-loss/15-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/comparing-predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: ce68be05102e6e996f44b908b48670e50377114a9229081029c3a74d95000f21; role: concept -->

Thus, the interval is useful for the paired-loss lesson, not a full confirmatory analysis of the experiment.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The conditional bootstrap resamples the stored verb differences while holding the fitted cross-validation predictions fixed. It respects verb as the resampling unit, but it does not reproduce participant, item, or refitting uncertainty. The population models also omit participant and sentence-item effects. Thus, the interval is useful for the paired-loss lesson, not a full confirmatory analysis of the experiment.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/005282/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-orientation/mega-orientation-v1.1.zip
:::

## Scope of the gain

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/comparing-predictive-loss/16-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/comparing-predictive-loss.qmd; note-sha256: ce68be05102e6e996f44b908b48670e50377114a9229081029c3a74d95000f21; role: concept -->

It does not turn acceptability into a directly observed temporal-orientation label, reproduce Moon and White's lexical-versus-structural theory comparison, or generalize to unrestricted English embedding verbs.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The interaction gain suggests that frame-specific orientation patterns help predict ratings for unseen verbs within this selected inventory. It does not turn acceptability into a directly observed temporal-orientation label, reproduce Moon and White's lexical-versus-structural theory comparison, or generalize to unrestricted English embedding verbs.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/005282/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-orientation/mega-orientation-v1.1.zip
:::

A paired comparison evaluates two models on identical held-out groups and returns their differences to the unit specified by the scientific claim. The previous page developed grouped splitting with Natural Stories. The next page begins a five-page Provo sequence using two fixed Gaussian mean models.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/005282/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-orientation/mega-orientation-v1.1.zip
:::

It is a fitted cloze estimate, not a language-model probability.

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests/09-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd; note-sha256: 832f5655baf4825341a06ac4e7741303261ddb387f408810785f17e1037c7586; role: math -->

$$

## From a likelihood ratio to a difference {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests/10-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd; note-sha256: 832f5655baf4825341a06ac4e7741303261ddb387f408810785f17e1037c7586; role: math -->

The likelihood-ratio statistic is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Lambda
&=-2\log\left(\frac{\widehat L_L}{\widehat L_Q}\right)\\
&=-2(\log\widehat L_L-\log\widehat L_Q)\\
&=2(\ell_Q-\ell_L).
\end{aligned}
$$

When the expanded model adds regular parameters and the usual large-sample conditions hold,

$$
\Lambda\overset{\cdot}{\sim}\chi^2_{k_Q-k_L}
$$

under the restricted model.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The likelihood-ratio statistic is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Lambda
&=-2\log\left(\frac{\widehat L_L}{\widehat L_Q}\right)\\
&=-2(\log\widehat L_L-\log\widehat L_Q)\\
&=2(\ell_Q-\ell_L).
\end{aligned}
$$

When the expanded model adds regular parameters and the usual large-sample conditions hold,

$$
\Lambda\overset{\cdot}{\sim}\chi^2_{k_Q-k_L}
$$

under the restricted model.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
https://osf.io/sjefs/
:::

## When the reference distribution may fail

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests/19-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd; note-sha256: 832f5655baf4825341a06ac4e7741303261ddb387f408810785f17e1037c7586; role: concept -->

In such cases, a simulation-based reference distribution or a method derived for the boundary problem may be needed.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The $\chi^2$ approximation assumes that the null value is an interior, regular point and that parameters are sufficiently identified. Testing a random-effect variance against zero violates this condition because zero is a boundary. Mixture models can lose component identification under a null restriction. In such cases, a simulation-based reference distribution or a method derived for the boundary problem may be needed.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
https://osf.io/sjefs/
:::

## Likelihood comparison and predictive validation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests/21-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd; note-sha256: 832f5655baf4825341a06ac4e7741303261ddb387f408810785f17e1037c7586; role: concept -->

These are different pieces of evidence.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The LRT uses the same responses to estimate and compare the models. Cross-validation asks how the complete procedures predict responses excluded from fitting. A quadratic term can pass an LRT while changing held-out prediction only slightly, or a proxy can improve prediction without supporting its proposed mechanism. These are different pieces of evidence.

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4

## Penalizing in-sample fit

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/02-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

This lets the penalty, rather than a change in data or response, explain any disagreement.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The likelihood-ratio page fixed a Provo position table and two nested Gaussian mean models. Information criteria use those same likelihoods but replace null-hypothesis calibration with a penalty for estimated flexibility. This lets the penalty, rather than a change in data or response, explain any disagreement.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Penalizing in-sample fit

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/03-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

Its score is relative to compatible candidates; the absolute value has no standalone linguistic unit.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **optimism of training error** is the fact that performance on observations used for fitting tends to be better than expected performance on new observations. An **information criterion** estimates a correction by combining fitted likelihood with a complexity penalty. Its score is relative to compatible candidates; the absolute value has no standalone linguistic unit.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## AIC: fit plus a parameter-count penalty {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/04-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: math -->

Let $\ell$ be maximized log likelihood and $k$ the number of likelihood parameters. The **Akaike information criterion (AIC)** is

$$
\operatorname{AIC}=2k-2\ell
=
\underbrace{-2\ell}_{\text{lack of fitted likelihood}}
+
\underbrace{2k}_{\text{complexity penalty}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $\ell$ be maximized log likelihood and $k$ the number of likelihood parameters. The **Akaike information criterion (AIC)** is

$$
\operatorname{AIC}=2k-2\ell
=
\underbrace{-2\ell}_{\text{lack of fitted likelihood}}
+
\underbrace{2k}_{\text{complexity penalty}}.
$$

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## AIC: fit plus a parameter-count penalty

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/05-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

The penalty is motivated as an approximation to relative expected predictive discrepancy, not as a significance threshold.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Greater maximized log likelihood lowers the first term; additional parameters increase the second. Lower AIC is preferred. The penalty is motivated as an approximation to relative expected predictive discrepancy, not as a significance threshold.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## BIC: a different penalty and motivation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/06-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: math -->

The **Bayesian information criterion (BIC)** is

$$
\operatorname{BIC}=k\log n-2\ell,
$$

where $n$ is the sample size supplied to the approximation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **Bayesian information criterion (BIC)** is

$$
\operatorname{BIC}=k\log n-2\ell,
$$

where $n$ is the sample size supplied to the approximation.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf

## BIC: a different penalty and motivation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/07-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

BIC is not merely a universally stricter AIC: it arises from a different approximation connected to model evidence under additional assumptions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Its penalty grows with $\log n$. BIC is not merely a universally stricter AIC: it arises from a different approximation connected to model evidence under additional assumptions.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## BIC: a different penalty and motivation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/08-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

It cannot convert those positions into independent readers or passages.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Repeated linguistic data can make the meaning of $n$ delicate. The Provo teaching table contains position summaries rather than reader-level observations, so its criterion calculation uses the number of retained positions. It cannot convert those positions into independent readers or passages.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## The Provo criterion disagreement

The empirical disagreement follows from applying different penalties to a modest fitted-likelihood gain.

## Keeping responses and observations fixed

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/13-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

Their printed values are not directly comparable without accounting for the transformation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Information criteria compare models only when their likelihoods concern the same observed responses. A model of raw duration and a model of log duration assign density to different response variables. Their printed values are not directly comparable without accounting for the transformation.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Keeping responses and observations fixed

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/14-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

Equal row counts alone would not establish that the same positions were used.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Candidate models can also silently use different rows when an added predictor has missing values. the calculation thus checks the row names in both model frames. Equal row counts alone would not establish that the same positions were used.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## What the criteria do not encode

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/15-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

BIC likewise cannot distinguish another position in an observed passage from a position in a passage absent during fitting.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

AIC approximates observation-level expected performance under its regularity conditions. It does not create held-out predictions or know which linguistic group should be new. BIC likewise cannot distinguish another position in an observed passage from a position in a passage absent during fitting.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## What the criteria do not encode

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/16-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

Here the criteria compare two compatible likelihood models for the fixed aggregated position table.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The position count also does not license reader-level or passage-level inference. Direct grouped validation is preferable when prediction for a wholly new passage is the target. Here the criteria compare two compatible likelihood models for the fixed aggregated position table.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## What the criteria do not encode

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria/17-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd; note-sha256: 9afe720d8fa6eff3e93f51f1034e809e6c207529a528c4da54a7a71238d16412; role: concept -->

It does not certify that the preferred candidate is an adequate explanation of the response process.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An information-criterion difference is not a conventional significance threshold. It ranks specified candidates under its approximation. It does not certify that the preferred candidate is an adequate explanation of the response process.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Leaving out one unit at a time

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation/02-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 231466fce0ba67809d9d559e40222edee96bb848e741543a108b702d559f9996; role: concept -->

The word *one* matters: here it means one Provo content-word position summary, conditional on all other positions, including positions from the same passage.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The information-criteria page approximated predictive discrepancy without constructing omitted-data predictions. **Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV)** instead makes one unit the test set at a time. The word *one* matters: here it means one Provo content-word position summary, conditional on all other positions, including positions from the same passage.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

## Defining the rotation {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation/03-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 231466fce0ba67809d9d559e40222edee96bb848e741543a108b702d559f9996; role: math -->

Let the data contain $N$ position summaries. For each position $i$, fit the complete procedure to the data with $i$ removed. Write the fitted predictor as

$$
\widehat f_{-i}
$$

and its prediction as

$$
\widehat y_{-i}=\widehat f_{-i}(x_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let the data contain $N$ position summaries. For each position $i$, fit the complete procedure to the data with $i$ removed. Write the fitted predictor as

$$
\widehat f_{-i}
$$

and its prediction as

$$
\widehat y_{-i}=\widehat f_{-i}(x_i).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

## Defining the rotation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation/04-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 231466fce0ba67809d9d559e40222edee96bb848e741543a108b702d559f9996; role: math -->

For a chosen loss $L$, the leave-one-out risk estimate is

$$
\widehat R_{\mathrm{LOO}}
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^N
L(y_i,\widehat y_{-i}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a chosen loss $L$, the leave-one-out risk estimate is

$$
\widehat R_{\mathrm{LOO}}
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^N
L(y_i,\widehat y_{-i}).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

The Bayesian calculation fixes a normal-inverse-gamma prior before any position is omitted.

::: {.notes}

We use the same Provo position table and Gaussian mean models as on the preceding pages. The Bayesian calculation fixes a normal-inverse-gamma prior before any position is omitted.

## Exact Bayesian LOO for the Provo models

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation/07-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 231466fce0ba67809d9d559e40222edee96bb848e741543a108b702d559f9996; role: concept -->

The inverse-gamma shape is a fixed computational setting, and its rate follows from the declared residual-variance mean.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The source paper reports excluding fixations shorter than 80 ms and longer than 800 ms. Their log-scale midpoint sets the prior intercept mean; slope means are zero. The expected residual variance treats four standard deviations as spanning those study bounds, and each coefficient's conditional prior variance multiplier is derived from the same span. The inverse-gamma shape is a fixed computational setting, and its rate follows from the declared residual-variance mean.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

It is a teaching prior, not a prior proposed by Luke and Christianson.

## What one means here

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation/12-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 231466fce0ba67809d9d559e40222edee96bb848e741543a108b702d559f9996; role: concept -->

It is not a new passage, reader, participant response, or word type.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

One omitted unit is a content-word position summary. Other positions from the same passage remain in the training data, and the response already averages over readers. The target is thus one position summary conditional on the remaining position table. It is not a new passage, reader, participant response, or word type.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

## What one means here

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation/13-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 231466fce0ba67809d9d559e40222edee96bb848e741543a108b702d559f9996; role: concept -->

A passage target requires leave-one-passage-out validation from the start.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The distinction persists even though every position receives an out-of-sample prediction. Summing pointwise scores within a passage would not retroactively remove that passage from fitting. A passage target requires leave-one-passage-out validation from the start.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

Conjugacy makes all 1593 Provo calculations available analytically.

## Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo/02-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo.qmd; note-sha256: c06a86dfc485e3884c7e58ee97ced4ddb5e32d8614e3f307f5f6b447f48488f6; role: concept -->

Because exact values are available here, approximation error becomes observable.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The exact LOO page computed every omitted-position posterior directly under a conjugate Provo model. **Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO)** approximates those omitted-data posteriors using draws from the posterior fit to all observations. Because exact values are available here, approximation error becomes observable.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/articles/online-only/faq.html
https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/pareto-k-diagnostic.html
:::

## Exact Bayesian leave-one-out prediction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo/03-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo.qmd; note-sha256: c06a86dfc485e3884c7e58ee97ced4ddb5e32d8614e3f307f5f6b447f48488f6; role: math -->

Let $y_{-i}$ contain all responses except $y_i$. Given a factorized likelihood and prior density $f(\theta)$,

$$
f(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\propto
f(\theta)\prod_{j\neq i}f(y_j\mid\theta).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $y_{-i}$ contain all responses except $y_i$. Given a factorized likelihood and prior density $f(\theta)$,

$$
f(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\propto
f(\theta)\prod_{j\neq i}f(y_j\mid\theta).
$$

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/articles/online-only/faq.html
https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/pareto-k-diagnostic.html
:::

## Exact Bayesian leave-one-out prediction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo/04-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo.qmd; note-sha256: c06a86dfc485e3884c7e58ee97ced4ddb5e32d8614e3f307f5f6b447f48488f6; role: math -->

The exact predictive density is

$$
f(y_i\mid y_{-i})
=
\int f(y_i\mid\theta)f(\theta\mid y_{-i})\,\mathrm d\theta.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The exact predictive density is

$$
f(y_i\mid y_{-i})
=
\int f(y_i\mid\theta)f(\theta\mid y_{-i})\,\mathrm d\theta.
$$

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/articles/online-only/faq.html
https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/pareto-k-diagnostic.html
:::

Summing its logarithm gives expected log pointwise predictive density:

$$
\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{loo}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^N\log f(y_i\mid y_{-i}).
$$

$$

## Relating the omitted posterior to the full posterior {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo/07-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo.qmd; note-sha256: c06a86dfc485e3884c7e58ee97ced4ddb5e32d8614e3f307f5f6b447f48488f6; role: math -->

Given draws $\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(S)}$ from

$$
f(\theta\mid y)
\propto
f(\theta)\prod_{j=1}^Nf(y_j\mid\theta),
$$

removing the $i$th contribution gives

$$
f(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\propto
\frac{f(\theta\mid y)}{f(y_i\mid\theta)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Given draws $\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(S)}$ from

$$
f(\theta\mid y)
\propto
f(\theta)\prod_{j=1}^Nf(y_j\mid\theta),
$$

removing the $i$th contribution gives

$$
f(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\propto
\frac{f(\theta\mid y)}{f(y_i\mid\theta)}.
$$

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/articles/online-only/faq.html
https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/pareto-k-diagnostic.html
:::

The raw importance ratio is consequently

$$
r_i^{(s)}\propto\frac{1}{f(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})}.
$$

A few enormous ratios can make full-posterior draws a poor representation of the omitted posterior.

This inverse weighting is both the shortcut and its weakness. A few enormous ratios can make full-posterior draws a poor representation of the omitted posterior.

## Relating the omitted posterior to the full posterior

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo/10-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo.qmd; note-sha256: c06a86dfc485e3884c7e58ee97ced4ddb5e32d8614e3f307f5f6b447f48488f6; role: concept -->

Large $k$ warns about the approximation; it does not establish that an observation is erroneous or should be removed.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

PSIS fits a generalized Pareto distribution to the largest ratios and replaces extreme values with smoothed ones. The **Pareto $k$ diagnostic** reports the fitted tail shape for each position. Large $k$ warns about the approximation; it does not establish that an observation is erroneous or should be removed.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/articles/online-only/faq.html
https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/pareto-k-diagnostic.html
:::

A vector of total log likelihoods cannot support omission because it discards the pointwise contributions.

## The pointwise likelihood fixes the target

A new-passage target would require a grouped likelihood and validation design from the start.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Default PSIS-LOO omits one such contribution. Here that contribution is one aggregated content-word position. Other positions from the same passage remain in the full posterior, so summing position scores by passage cannot create leave-one-passage-out validation. A new-passage target would require a grouped likelihood and validation design from the start.

## The widely applicable information criterion

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic/02-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.qmd; note-sha256: a973df373f1b0f5fd2deebb36f4f51e68ce762ece1caf2752f1d51d39ca36ab4; role: concept -->

Both calculations require the same pointwise likelihood matrix, but their approximations differ.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The PSIS-LOO page used full-posterior draws to approximate omitted-position posteriors. The **widely applicable information criterion (WAIC)** instead corrects fitted pointwise posterior predictive density using posterior variation. Both calculations require the same pointwise likelihood matrix, but their approximations differ.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::

## Fitted posterior predictive density {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic/03-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.qmd; note-sha256: a973df373f1b0f5fd2deebb36f4f51e68ce762ece1caf2752f1d51d39ca36ab4; role: math -->

For observation $i$, the **log pointwise predictive density (lppd)** is

$$
\operatorname{lppd}_i
=
\log\left[
\frac{1}{S}
\sum_{s=1}^S
f(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})
\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For observation $i$, the **log pointwise predictive density (lppd)** is

$$
\operatorname{lppd}_i
=
\log\left[
\frac{1}{S}
\sum_{s=1}^S
f(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})
\right].
$$

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::

## Fitted posterior predictive density {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic/04-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.qmd; note-sha256: a973df373f1b0f5fd2deebb36f4f51e68ce762ece1caf2752f1d51d39ca36ab4; role: math -->

The average integrates the likelihood of $y_i$ over posterior uncertainty. But $y_i$ helped determine the posterior, so this remains a fitted predictive quantity. Summing gives

$$
\operatorname{lppd}=\sum_{i=1}^N\operatorname{lppd}_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The average integrates the likelihood of $y_i$ over posterior uncertainty. But $y_i$ helped determine the posterior, so this remains a fitted predictive quantity. Summing gives

$$
\operatorname{lppd}=\sum_{i=1}^N\operatorname{lppd}_i.
$$

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::

## The pointwise optimism correction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic/05-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.qmd; note-sha256: a973df373f1b0f5fd2deebb36f4f51e68ce762ece1caf2752f1d51d39ca36ab4; role: math -->

WAIC estimates effective flexibility from the posterior variance of each pointwise log likelihood:

$$
p_{\mathrm{waic},i}
=
\operatorname{Var}_s\left[
\log f(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})
\right],
$$

and

$$
p_{\mathrm{waic}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^Np_{\mathrm{waic},i}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

WAIC estimates effective flexibility from the posterior variance of each pointwise log likelihood:

$$
p_{\mathrm{waic},i}
=
\operatorname{Var}_s\left[
\log f(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})
\right],
$$

and

$$
p_{\mathrm{waic}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^Np_{\mathrm{waic},i}.
$$

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::

## The pointwise optimism correction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic/06-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.qmd; note-sha256: a973df373f1b0f5fd2deebb36f4f51e68ce762ece1caf2752f1d51d39ca36ab4; role: math -->

The effective count depends on the fitted posterior, not merely on the number of regression coefficients. WAIC's expected log predictive density is

$$
\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}}
=
\operatorname{lppd}-p_{\mathrm{waic}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The effective count depends on the fitted posterior, not merely on the number of regression coefficients. WAIC's expected log predictive density is

$$
\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}}
=
\operatorname{lppd}-p_{\mathrm{waic}}.
$$

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::

## The pointwise optimism correction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic/07-math; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.qmd; note-sha256: a973df373f1b0f5fd2deebb36f4f51e68ce762ece1caf2752f1d51d39ca36ab4; role: math -->

Larger values are preferred. The deviance-scale quantity is

$$
\operatorname{WAIC}=-2\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}},
$$

for which smaller is preferred.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Larger values are preferred. The deviance-scale quantity is

$$
\operatorname{WAIC}=-2\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}},
$$

for which smaller is preferred.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::

## What the correction does not change

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic/12-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.qmd; note-sha256: a973df373f1b0f5fd2deebb36f4f51e68ce762ece1caf2752f1d51d39ca36ab4; role: concept -->

Other positions from the same passage remain part of the fitted posterior used to calculate each contribution.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

WAIC is tied to the unit represented by one likelihood column. Here that unit is an aggregated content-word position. The correction does not create prediction for a wholly new reader, word type, or passage. Other positions from the same passage remain part of the fitted posterior used to calculate each contribution.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::

## What the correction does not change

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic/13-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.qmd; note-sha256: a973df373f1b0f5fd2deebb36f4f51e68ce762ece1caf2752f1d51d39ca36ab4; role: concept -->

PSIS-LOO is often easier to diagnose because Pareto $k$ targets its importance-sampling approximation directly.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Large posterior variance in a pointwise log likelihood can warn that WAIC is unreliable for that position. The warning concerns the approximation; it does not license discarding a linguistically surprising point. PSIS-LOO is often easier to diagnose because Pareto $k$ targets its importance-sampling approximation directly.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::

## What the correction does not change

<!-- generated-slide-id: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic/14-concept; notes-page: model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.qmd; note-sha256: a973df373f1b0f5fd2deebb36f4f51e68ce762ece1caf2752f1d51d39ca36ab4; role: concept -->

It does not establish that the preferred predictor causes the reading response or explains the linguistic process that produced it.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Finally, WAIC ranks compatible candidate models. It does not establish that the preferred predictor causes the reading response or explains the linguistic process that produced it.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::
